extracted.intended_audience: Users of the Magma computer algebra system (mathematicians / computational algebraists) working with multivariate polynomial rings, ideals, quotient rings, and series
extracted.subtask_description: Reference documentation for Magma's multivariate polynomial rings module: how ideals, Groebner bases, quotient rings, varieties, radicals/decompositions, graded rings/Hilbert series, dimension, and power/Laurent series are defined and the functions to compute with them. Includes usage notes, definitions, and examples for correct construction and computation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal constructor and basis management
rubrics_metrics.description: Magma's ideal constructor is given a polynomial ring P (or an over-ideal) and a list describing a basis. Magma remembers the original basis as the current basis for the ideal until it needs a GrÃ¶bner basis; at that point it changes the current basis to the unique GrÃ¶bner basis and discards the original basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To force explicit computation of the GrÃ¶bner basis call Groebner(I), but this is normally unnecessary because Magma computes the GrÃ¶bner basis automatically when required. Example shows initial printed basis versus printed Groebner basis after computation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forcing and controlling Groebner computations
rubrics_metrics.description: Groebner(I) may be invoked to force computation of an ideal's GrÃ¶bner basis; SetVerbose("Groebner",1) gives verbose output for the Buchberger algorithm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normally unnecessary to call Groebner explicitly. Use SetVerbose("Groebner",1) to see Buchberger steps; verbosity can be increased further where supported.

rubrics_metrics.name: GrÃ¶bner Walk algorithm and ChangeOrder
rubrics_metrics.description: Magma implements the GrÃ¶bner Walk algorithm for changing a GrÃ¶bner basis from one monomial order to another; typically compute GrÃ¶bner basis under an easy order (e.g., grevlex) then use GrÃ¶bner Walk to convert to desired order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This two-step method is generally faster than running Buchberger directly in the final order. The ChangeOrder function allows manually applying the GrÃ¶bner Walk. The method is used automatically whenever a GrÃ¶bner basis is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disabling GrÃ¶bner Walk for Groebner
rubrics_metrics.description: The Walk parameter controls whether GrÃ¶bner Walk is used: Groebner(I : Walk := false) constructs the GrÃ¶bner basis without using the GrÃ¶bner Walk algorithm, using Buchberger directly with the final order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when the Walk approach is slower for a particular ideal. Verbose output for the GrÃ¶bner Walk is enabled via SetVerbose("GroebnerWalk",1); verbosity level 2 also enables Buchberger printing inside the walk (normally suppressed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic ideal access and arithmetic functions
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of canonical ideal operations are provided (I + J, I*J, I^k, ColonIdeal(I,J), ColonIdeal(I,f), I meet J, &meet S, Generic(I), I eq J, I subset J, IsProper(I), IsZero(I), f in I, IsInRadical(f,I), NormalForm(f,I), SPolynomial(f,g) ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each function performs the standard algebraic operation (sum, product, power, colon ideal/quotient, intersection, generic polynomial, equality, containment, properness, zero ideal test, membership, radical membership test, normal form reduction, S-polynomial). Examples show usage (meet, subset checks, product equality) and membership vs radical membership distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotient ring construction and interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotient rings Q = P/I can be created with / or quo; Q consists of residues (normal forms) of P modulo I and has vector space structure over the coefficient field K.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
New indeterminates of Q may be named using angle bracket notation. Construction via quo

and via P / I are equivalent. Use VectorSpace(Q) to obtain an isomorphic vector space and isomorphism useful for structural investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotient-ring related functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Functions available: CoefficientRing(Q), Rank(Q), Q.i, Dimension(Q), VectorSpace(Q) (with isomorphism), MatrixAlgebra(Q) (with isomorphism), RepresentationMatrix(f), MinimalPolynomial(f), IsUnit(f), IsNilpotent(f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These functions let you inspect structural invariants (rank/dimension), access indeterminates, convert Q to vector/matrix algebras, and test or compute properties of elements (minimal polynomial, unit/nilpotent status). Examples show obtaining basis and minimal polynomial computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elimination ideals and triangularization property
rubrics_metrics.description: For an ideal I in K[x1,..,xn] and integer k with 0 <= k < n, the k-th elimination ideal Ik = I ∩ K[x_{k+1},..,x_n]. If B is a GrÃ¶bner basis for I w.r.t lexicographical order x1 > ... > xn, then B ∩ K[x_{k+1},..,x_n] is a GrÃ¶bner basis of Ik (GrÃ¶bner bases 'triangularize' systems).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use EliminationIdeal(I,k) to compute the k-th elimination ideal. EliminationIdeal(I,S) eliminates all variables except those in S. Examples show elimination producing basis polynomials and verifying membership in I.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zero-dimensional ideal characterization and test
rubrics_metrics.description: An ideal I is zero-dimensional iff the quotient P/I has finite dimension as a vector space over K (equivalently the variety over algebraic closure is finite).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use IsZeroDimensional(I) to test. When zero-dimensional, univariate elimination ideals I ∩ K[x_i] are non-trivial and have unique monic generators. Examples demonstrate detection and subsequent computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Univariate elimination generators and efficient computation
rubrics_metrics.description: UnivariateEliminationIdealGenerator(I,i) returns the unique monic generator of the i-th univariate elimination ideal; UnivariateEliminationIdealGenerators(I) returns all n generators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magma computes one GrÃ¶bner basis under an easy order and then applies the GrÃ¶bner Walk to an elimination order to obtain these generators efficiently; this is generally much faster than linear-algebra based methods. Examples print large univariate polynomials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computing varieties and extension-field behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Variety(I) returns the variety of I as a sorted sequence of vectors in K^n; VarietySequence(I) returns sequence-of-sequences for clearer printing. Variants Variety(I,L) and VarietySequence(I,L) compute over extension field L; the variety over an extension may include additional solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use VarietySizeOverAlgebraicClosure(I) to obtain number of solutions over algebraic closure. Examples show computing variety over Q and over a quadratic extension and comparing sizes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Radical of an ideal and computation
rubrics_metrics.description: The radical R of I is { f | f^k ∈ I for some k >= 1 } and is the largest ideal containing I with same variety. Radical(I) computes the radical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Computing the radical often yields simpler structure to understand the variety; verbose output for the radical algorithm via SetVerbose("Radical",1). Examples show conversion of a non-zero-dimensional ideal to a simpler radical ideal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Radical decomposition into prime ideals
rubrics_metrics.description: Any radical ideal decomposes uniquely (up to ordering) into a minimal intersection of prime ideals. RadicalDecomposition(I) computes the radical R and returns the minimal sorted sequence of prime ideals whose intersection is R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prime decomposition of radical corresponds to decomposition of variety into irreducible components; examples illustrate two prime components and their Groebner bases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary decomposition and associated primes
rubrics_metrics.description: A (not necessarily radical) ideal I can be decomposed into an intersection of primary ideals; for each primary ideal J in the decomposition its radical is a prime ideal called an associated prime. PrimaryDecomposition(I) returns primary components and associated primes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Associated primes may contain other associated primes; the function returns both sequences. Examples show a decomposition of size 8 and list bases for primary components and associated primes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tests for radical, primary, prime, maximal
rubrics_metrics.description: Boolean functions: IsRadical(I) true iff I equals its radical; IsPrimary(I) true iff I is primary; IsPrime(I) true iff I is prime; IsMaximal(I) true iff I is maximal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These tests let users inspect algebraic properties of computed ideals; Table 22.6 lists these functions alongside Radical/Decomposition functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighted (graded) polynomial rings and weights
rubrics_metrics.description: PolynomialRing(R,Q) creates a graded polynomial ring with variable weights given by Q = [d1,...,dn]. A monomial x1^{e1} ... xn^{en} has weighted degree sum(ei*di). A ring with no specified weights assumes weight 1 for each variable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Printout includes 'Variable weights: ...'. Use WeightedDegree(f) for weighted degree, LeadingWeightedDegree(f) for leading monomial's weighted degree. Examples show weighted degrees and contrast with total degree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homogeneity tests for polynomials and ideals
rubrics_metrics.description: IsHomogeneous(f) returns whether polynomial f is homogeneous w.r.t. variable weights. IsHomogeneous(I) returns whether ideal I is homogeneous (i.e., has a basis of homogeneous polynomials).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Homogeneity is with respect to weights; examples show true/false cases and constructing a homogeneous ideal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hilbert series and Hilbert polynomial computations
rubrics_metrics.description: For homogeneous ideal I in graded ring P, the Hilbert series H_{P/I}(t) = sum_{d>=0} dim(V_d) t^d is returned by HilbertSeries(I) as an element of a univariate function field. If all weights are 1, there exists a Hilbert polynomial F_{P/I}(d) equal to coefficients of t^i for all i >= k for some k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: HilbertPolynomial(I) returns the polynomial and the index of regularity k. Examples demonstrate computing series, converting to power series, and checking evaluations of polynomial against coefficients for i>=k.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dimension of an ideal (combinatorial definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A subset U of variables X is independent modulo I if I ∩ K[U] = ∅; maximally independent sets determine dimension. The dimension of I is the maximum cardinality of independent sets modulo I (dimension 0 corresponds to zero-dimensional ideal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dimension(I) returns the integer dimension d and a sorted sequence U of variable indices giving a maximally independent set. Example: I = <x, y^2> in K[x,y,z] has dimension 1 with maximally independent set {z}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power series and Laurent series core definitions and precision model
rubrics_metrics.description: Power series have form a_v x^v + a_{v+1} x^{v+1} + ... with v >= 0; Laurent series allow finite negative powers. Because of finite memory, Magma stores series truncated as a_v x^v + ... + a_{p-1} x^{p-1} + O(x^p). Valuation(f) returns least exponent v with nonzero coefficient; AbsolutePrecision(f) returns p; RelativePrecision = p - v; Degree(f) returns last known nonzero exponent d; Coefficients(f) returns [a_v,...,a_d]; Coefficient(f,i) returns coefficient of x^i; Truncate(f) removes O term to make exact series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exact series have finite number of nonzero terms. Note the difference in Coefficients ordering for series (starts at valuation) vs polynomials. Special behavior for exact zero and approximate zero O(x^p) is noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing series rings and elements (free precision)
rubrics_metrics.description:
PowerSeriesRing(R) (or LaurentSeriesRing(R)) creates a free-precision series ring where each element may have its own precision. Exact elements can be given like polynomials; elements with finite absolute precision are created using O(x^p). elt< P | v, Q, r > constructs element with valuation v, coefficient sequence Q and relative precision r; omitting v sets valuation 0, omitting r sets relative precision to length(Q), r = -1 makes an exact series. Coercion from sequence behaves like elt

.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructed examples show elt usage and coercions; negative valuations allowed in Laurent series. Inverses and other operations producing infinite series are truncated according to ring precision attribute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision attribute for free series rings and changing precision
rubrics_metrics.description: Free series rings have a 'Precision' attribute giving the default relative precision used when unbounded computations occur. HasAttribute(P,'Precision') returns (true, value). AssertAttribute(P,'Precision',p) changes the attribute for newly-created elements only; existing elements keep their precision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Default precision for free rings is 20 unless set otherwise. Example shows changing precision to 28 affects subsequently-created elements but not previously-created ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specifying default precision at ring construction
rubrics_metrics.description: When creating a free series ring you may set Precision via a parameter: e.g., PowerSeriesRing(Q: Precision := 8) or LaurentSeriesRing(Q: Precision := 8) to set default relative precision for the ring at creation time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show resulting truncated expansions reflecting the chosen precision. This controls how many terms operations like division produce by default.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed absolute precision power series rings
rubrics_metrics.description: PowerSeriesRing(R,p) creates a power series ring of fixed absolute precision p: all elements have absolute precision p (behaves like quotient R[[x]]/x^p). Precision(P) returns p and s^k prints as s^k + O(s^p).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elements printed reflect the fixed precision (e.g., s^5 prints with O(s^p)). The fixed-precision model ensures all elements have the same absolute precision and is useful when a uniform truncation bound is desired.
